findings.criterion: 2. One route table, declarative auth, default-deny.
findings.section: Wave 9 — W9 — Auth Enforce + Cookie Navigation + Ops Cutover (C2 gate)
findings.message: Wave 9 specifies that the `anchor_auth` cookie is `HttpOnly` (preventing JS access) yet allows a fallback to `?token=` on WebSocket/SSE connections. If the token is not exposed to JS, the client cannot construct the fallback URL; if the token is exposed to JS (e.g., via `window.ANCHOR_BOOT`), it defeats the security isolation of the `HttpOnly` cookie.

findings.section: Wave 12 — journal.py Core: emit() Choke Point + Butler Envelope
findings.message: By requiring explicit operator action to replay/confirm unconfirmed intents rather than automatically reconciling them on startup (e.g., auto-confirming if the legacy write is verified to have succeeded), any crash in the legacy-to-confirm window leaves the journal permanently incomplete. If a rebuild occurs before manual operator intervention, the recovery tool will omit these writes, failing the 'recoverable-by-construction' guarantee.

findings.section: Wave 15 — Supervisor Core: Inline Seam + IPC Contract + Restart Matrix
findings.message: Since the supervisor must run with 'Python stdlib only' and the restarted supervisor is not the OS-level parent of the surviving jobs, it cannot use standard parent-child signals or `subprocess` APIs. Monitoring non-child processes on Windows without third-party libraries requires complex `ctypes` bindings to open handles and poll exit codes. If a job terminates while the supervisor is restarting, the exit code cannot be retrieved, violating clean job status tracking.

findings.section: Wave 9 — W9 — Auth Enforce + Cookie Navigation + Ops Cutover (C2 gate)
findings.message: Since the `boot_secret` is minted per server start, any dashboard restart (including the supervisor restart demo or daily service cycles) invalidates all active browser and PWA cookies. Because cookieless/tokenless page hits return a hard 401 error page instead of delegating to a local token-read or auto-refresh handshake, John's existing open tabs will break and require manual relaunch from desktop files, disrupting daily use.

Under the proposed dual-write policy, if a crash occurs after the legacy write succeeds but before the CONFIRM marker is appended, the legacy store contains the mutated data but the journal only has the unconfirmed INTENT. Because the parity gate classifies this divergence as "OK-with-report" and the rebuild tool only consumes CONFIRMED events, rebuilding a deleted index.json will discard this valid, completed user mutation. This violates Success Criterion 3 by failing to recover a completed write from the journal. The reconciler should automatically promote/confirm such intents if the legacy store check passes, rather than relying on manual operator intervention while tolerating data-loss-vulnerable states as "OK".

If the ConPTY spike is successful (verdict YES), deferring PTY adoption to a follow-up effort (option ii) while leaving PTYs dashboard-owned violates Success Criterion 4 and the locked North Star Objective ("so the dashboard can restart without killing in-flight jobs or terminals"). A follow-up plan is only permitted if the spike refutes economic feasibility (verdict NO), or if a formal North-Star amendment is approved.

Running the supervisor service as `.\john` while the existing `anchor` dashboard service runs under a different account (e.g., LocalSystem) will cause Windows ACL permission conflicts in the shared `ANCHOR_DATA_DIR`. Since both processes must read and write to the same job records and event logs, the installer must ensure both services run under the same user account or explicitly configure inherited full-control ACLs on the relocated data directory.

Wave 9 combines the client-side bootstrapping changes (updating launchers to `/auth?token=`, setting the cookie) and the server-side auth enforcement in a single wave. Under the sequencing rule ("no auth flip ships in the same deploy as JS calling the flipped routes"), these must be deployed separately to prevent clients from receiving 401s during the rollout. Combining them in Wave 9 violates this safety rule and risks breaking the dashboard during deployment.

The draft states there is "never a token-entry form" and that all clients must authenticate via the `/auth?token=...` launcher URL. However, the iPhone PWA over Tailscale HTTPS (mentioned in W3/W9) cannot run Windows launcher scripts (.bat/.vbs/.pyw) and its static start URL cannot dynamically inject the Windows token. Without a token-entry form or alternative login method, remote/mobile clients are completely locked out after a cookie expires or server restarts.

Minting `boot_secret` per server start means any dashboard restart (e.g., `nssm restart anchor` to test/verify a change or run daily updates) invalidates all active cookies. While the split supervisor keeps the job running, the user's browser/PWA session will receive a 401 error and be forced to re-authenticate via the launcher. This breaks the seamless dashboard-restart experience required by Success Criterion 4.

In the three-step dual-write policy (intent -> legacy write -> confirm), if step 2 (legacy write) fails due to a validation error, permission issue, or lock conflict, the transaction is aborted and step 3 is never reached. This leaves a permanent unconfirmed intent in the journal that is indistinguishable from crash residue. On subsequent boots, the startup reconciler will surface this as crash residue, creating false positives and risk of accidental operator replay of invalid/failed mutations.

The supervisor installer `install_supervisor.ps1` clones `AppEnvironmentExtra` from the anchor service at install time. If `ANCHOR_TOKEN` or other configuration variables are updated on the anchor service later, the supervisor service's environment will fall out of sync, causing loopback IPC authentication failures.
